newsitem.title: CHINA: Asian Metals - China traders said offering copper.
newsitem.headline: Asian Metals - China traders said offering copper.

text.p: Chinese copper traders and producers have been offering copper onto the world market as prices for the red metal soar, metals traders in East Asia said on Monday.

A trader in Hong Kong with a Chinese state firm said he had been offered 1,000 tonnes of Chilean copper by Chinese merchants who did not want to take delivery of the metal because their own customers could not afford the current high prices.
Copper prices on the London Metal Exchange (LME) hit their highest point in almost a year on Friday, rising to $2,488 per tonne before easing back to close at $2,466.
The trading source said the Chinese merchants had offered him Chilean copper at the LME cash price, with no premium, for delivery to LME warehouses in Singapore.
This followed other recent offers by Chinese merchants keen on cashing in on the current rally.
A European trader in Singapore said the Chinese traders offering their metal were trying to consolidate profits, having bought the metal on forward contracts at low prices.
"If you sell into the domestic (Chinese) market it is sometimes difficult to get your money, or you get renminbi (yuan) when you need dollars to pay shippers," he said.
Sources inside and outside China said that as long as copper prices stayed above $2,200-2,300 a tonne, Chinese buyers would not be interested in stocking up on the metal.

The Chinese trader in Hong Kong said he had also been contacted by a Chinese cathode producer in the country's north offering to supply 500 tonnes a month of non-registered copper over the next six months.
"Of course they could sell it domestically, but they want foreign currency," he said, adding he would only sell the non-registered copper if he found a customer first.
Aluminium, by contrast, was providing one international trading house with a record year, an executive with the firm said without giving details.
He said aluminium ingots arriving in southern Chinese ports were fuelling the construction boom in southern China and were being bought by extruders, merchants and arbitrage traders.
The July aluminium contract on the Shanghai Metal Exchange opened at 15,820 yuan ($1,906) per tonne on Monday, against the LME's Friday close of $1,666.50.

The metal's rally on the LME of about $130 in the past couple of weeks has closed the arbitrage gap, another trader said, adding that most of the aluminium metal arriving in China is heading to construction and infrastructure sites.
Official figures show China's imports of unwrought aluminium and aluminium materials in the first quarter of 1997 reached 129,707 tonnes, down 0.3 percent from the same period in 1996.
With the LME the only source of the metal, prices were seen rising above $1,700 a tonne in the short term, traders said.
The market's tightness was seen as being caused by producers having oversold on long-term contracts or by traders having sold short, they said.
Heading into the peak summer season, the declines in aluminium stocks that have been the major feature of the current rally were expected to continue to support prices, traders said.
LME aluminium stocks fell 2,250 tonnes on Monday, figures released showed.
-- Shanghai newsroom (86-21) 6279-8544
